Latest Update: Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

In a recent development, it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Industry observers note that shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

Industry observers note that this massive-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and organization also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

Recent findings suggest that I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley indicates up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

It has been revealed that mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

Sources indicate that I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

Recent findings suggest that I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

According to recent reports, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

Sources indicate that this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

According to recent reports, A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition has been rated in Korea

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rating for the unannounced Nioh 3 Complete Edition has popped up on Korea's Game Rating and Administration Committee (GRAC).

As Insider Gaming spotted, the board gave Nioh 3 Complete Edition a 19+ rating on 17th November after it was submitted on 2nd November, even though Koei Tecmo hasn't revealed a Complete Edition for the game yet.

The listing, translated by machine, describes it as "a compilation of additional content from the dark Sengoku action RPG Nioh 3", and gives the rating for "excessive expression of violence", noting that "red blood and body amputation frequently occur during combat".

The listing also notes an overseas rating, which Insider Gaming claims is a 17+ rating from Japan's CERO.

Unlike some rating boards, GRAC publishes its ratings as soon as they're decided, which is why game listings often surface there before they're officially announced.

If Koei Tecmo follows the same pattern as Nioh 2, there may not be long to wait. GRAC's records show Nioh 2 was rated in January 2020, and its Complete Edition followed in November that year. Nioh 3 was rated on 14th November 2025, almost exactly a year ago.

It has been revealed that complete Editions typically includes the base game and all of its DLC. It could even launch alongside Nioh 3's second DLC, Bloody Insurrection, which is due in February 2027. Eurogamer has contacted Koei Tecmo for comment and we'll let you know if/when they come back to us.

Back in April, an update introduced "multiple high-difficulty Battle Scrolls" (side missions), accessible from shrines, the addition of a Stone of Penance item "which increases accessory +Values and rarities in exchange for higher difficulties", and upcoming skills given as rewards for completing the aforementioned high-level Battle Scroll missions.

Eurogamer's review of Nioh 3 called the threequel a new high for the 'masocore' series and "the crucible in which all of Team Ninja's experience has been siphoned into." It's sold over one million copies (and counting) since its 6th February launch.

Any official GTA 6 PC port’s ability to deliver a proper first person mode would be its biggest ace in the hole, so reckon I, a traitor

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that as Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been playing GTA 6 on PS5.

In a recent development, to be fair, I’ve made no secret of my looks to do just that if you’ve read any of our recent roundups of what everyone’s playing over the weekend. I can understand why it might leave a sour taste in the mouth, but it is what it is. No corporate gun has been pointed at my head as a mandate to temporarily forsake my PC and play the substantial game of the moment is forced into my hands.

Anyway, I’m writing about playing GTA 6 on console because it’s led me to conclude that a particular aspect of GTA 5’s PC port - one I’ve always rather taken for granted - could be a bigger deal for the inevitable Windows version of 6 than even the usual go-to PC plus points. You know, better graphics, superior performance, and modding. Historically, Rockstar’s crime sandboxes are games played from the third person perspective. That shot lingering behind Niko Bellic as he jogs around Brooklyn with a rocket launcher or following the damn bike of CJ as he in turn follows that damn train. This is the default way GTA’s breakneck action is presented to the player and was with GTA 5 at launch.

Sources indicate that as Rockstar’s offerings have shuffled away from arcadey rampage facilitators and ever deeper into the mould of uber-detailed life of crime sims, however, they've also began letting players see things directly through the eyes of the crim whose blood-splattered shoes they’ve stepped into. In order to do that, while simultaneously pushing the detail and graphical boundaries of their rendered worlds, Rockstar have needed to squeeze every bit of juice they can from the available hardware. Red Dead Redemption 2 managed to include a full first person mode at launch. GTA 6 hasn’t been so lucky, even if there are moments when bringing up your phone or reading a note temporarily lodges the camera into Jason and Lucia’s noggins.

According to recent reports, there is a way to glitch yourself into a more permanent first person perspective, but it’s naturally not got the polish that a proper first person mode would. What it does do is make clear that, with vehicle interiors lavishly detailed and some gun animations looking natural rather than janky, any port using the PC's extra horses to deliver a proper first person mode seems a no brainer, if not something already set in stone.

Assuming that is the case, I frankly can’t see why first person won’t become the go-to perspective on PC. Even more so than RDR2, GTA 6 feels like a game built to belong in first person. It dedicates so much time and energy to engaging you in every aspect of Jason and Lucia’s routines, rendering everything from eating to working out to doing up a house (and the acts involved in doing a robbery, I guess) in such exhaustive detail and depth that it’s almost beyond parody.

According to recent reports, notifications ping about you needing to finish a bench pressing session where every rep involves holding and releasing R2 and L2 at just the right time. An app tells you you’re hungry, so you wander over to the fridge, pick out a protein shake to down, then press R2 to lob the bottle in the bin, assuming you’re keen to keep your flat tidy. Shopping trips see you pick up groceries off shelves, stow them in a bag, then run home with it tucked under your arm because you’ve brought a motorbike and forgotten it lacks a boot. Every stickup begins with the ritual of picking your longarm gun out of your car’s boot, where it might have sat next to a bag of drugs you’ve stowed to deliver to a fence later. Stopping off to switch cars and clothes to throw the cops off your scent is no longer just for overenthusiastic roleplayers.

According to recent reports, the fact that the game goes to such lengths only to maintain the detachment inherent to the third person view feels bizarrely antithetical at times, like an exhibition of a tiny Fabergé egg that you’re forced to view through a telescope from the surface of Mars. The massive efforts of Rockstar’s developers - many of whom are presently trying to gain formal union recognition or have been fighting the company at an employment tribunal over firings they argue were unjust - went into putting together an artwork that regularly ends up at an arm’s length out of necessity, despite packing intricacies likely best seen through a magnifying glass.

Enter the PC release. And possibly nothing else offering the same bang for your buck around the same time. With GTA 5, the PS4 and Xbox One got an enhanced version of the game around the time of the PC port, offering a number of extra features - including a first person mode. Rockstar were quick to rule out GTA 6 getting 60 or 40fps performance modes on current console hardware due to a lack of horses, and if that also applies to a first person mode, then such a thing might only come with the next generation of consoles. That’d be the PS6 and Xbox’s Project Helix, neither of which seem hugely imminent and could well end up boasting ludicrous prices thanks to the ongoing memory shortages.

So, those who already own a PC capable of running any GTA 6 port could be in the best position to enjoy the game from a Jason and Lucia-eye view the moment such a thing becomes possible. Sure, it would also look and run better, but to be brutally honest I’ve found it looks damn gorgeous and runs acceptably on PS5. Sure, modding will no doubt spring up must-have additions, but the base game already works in plenty of the roleplaying mechanics and in-depth side-jobbing that a lot of popular GTA 5 mods delivered.

Sources indicate that thus, that window as the place to play GTA 6 as it feels intended, in first person, is what I’d right now peg as the best chance for the crimsim to be not just a great game you can play on PC - as I’d argue Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 5 are - but a great PC game that’s inarguably best experienced on our platform of choice. I don’t think writing that is falling into the trap it’s easy to end up in with significant games that hit console first: declaring in salesman-like fashion that they’ll of course be better on PC by default, in a manner that sometimes feels a bit like you’re trying to convince yourself that you’ve not paid more than a pre-RAM crisis console buyer for nothing.

Recent findings suggest that I’d never consider playing Cyberpunk 2077 in anything but first person on PC. GTA 6, from what I’ve played thus far, could be the next uber-detailed open world I spend hundreds of hours taking in the sights of, ideally through the eyes of a highly dangerous and highly stylish operator on the prowl for lucrative underworld opportunities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I hate to credit Sony's aggressive (and presumably very expensive) marketing campaign for GTA 6—you know, the one which appeared to have also plucked the ability for Xbox to even mention the game by name. That's something I'm still shocked was even a thing anyone was allowed to do.

According to recent reports, so I won't credit it… mostly. We all already know that PC is going to get the best version of GTA 6 when it finally hits our desktops, whenever that might be. But I am going to agree with one part of the whole "Grand Theft Auto 6 plays best on PS5" shtick: the DualSense controller. It's so good that I fear those who reach for a mouse and keyboard will be missing out on some incredible immersion.

It has been revealed that I never expected a controller to actively add to my experience, but I also forgot just how many goodies Sony stuffed into this thing. Seriously, Rockstar has taken full advantage of everything the peripheral has to offer.

I've been weaving through traffic way more in GTA 6 thanks to a huge increase in general vehicle density and some criminally narrow roads that can cause some major bottlenecks. Flooring it all the way from A to B isn't quite as easy as it used to be, which is why I kind of love how you can use the adaptive triggers to comfortably maintain a steady cruising speed before clicking it all the way in as a way to floor it. It makes my speed feel just that little more deliberate, with that tactile feel for when I really want to amp up how fast I'm going.

But driving might actually be the least interesting way Rockstar has made full use of the controller. The parts that have gotten me more than anything are the small ways haptics have been implemented to strengthen story moments or make parts of Leonida feel even more alive.

According to recent reports, the first time I really noticed the controller was back in the beginning of the game, when I'm instructed to go and pick Lucia up from prison. As I'm standing outside as Jason, watching her emerge from the gate, the controller starts thumping just a little bit. A heartbeat. I'm literally feeling Jason's heart racing as Lucia approaches. No dialogue, no internal monologue letting me know how nervous he is. It's such a small detail, but one that massively hammed up the moment for me.

My absolute favourite way it's been implemented, though? The clubs. The goddamn clubs. Leonida's sprawling nightlife is already impressive in isolation—Hitman's Berlin level was the last time I felt this enamoured with a videogame nightclub—but this is where Rockstar went all-in on the controller's haptic feedback. Step into a club and you'll immediately feel the bass pulsating through the controller.

Keep up to date with the most key stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Recent findings suggest that it's not just the same, monorhythmic beat for every song though. The bass perfectly matches the song; those long, teeth-shaking booms cut with shorter, less intense thumps. I feel like I'm back in my first year of university trying to sleep while the nearby student nightclub blasts the same songs until 3am every damn Wednesday, the bass somehow reverberating across the campus and straight through my bedframe.

In a recent development, when I first set foot inside the Jack of Hearts club at the beginning of Chapter 3, I was practically stunlocked by how much more immersive being able to feel the bass through the controller was making the entire experience. Seriously, I cannot overstate just how much it sucks you into what's happening around you.

According to recent reports, these are all things that I genuinely feel folks are going to miss out on with a simple mouse and keyboard. Sure, your aiming will be better. Yes, none of the things I've described above actually change anything about the gameplay. It'll still be the same GTA 6 no matter what you play with. But for all the ways Rockstar has managed to elevate the experience and the immersion I've been feeling just through something as small as the controller I'm holding? It at least deserves consideration for your go-to playthrough peripheral.

#121153. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow.
  • Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment.
  • Recent findings suggest that just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the upcoming movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a substantial eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”.

Recent findings suggest that just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the upcoming movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he says. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a major movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very notable for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

Sources indicate that francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she noted she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”.

I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

In a recent development, then I fly to New York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

That working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to Latest York to meet with Suzanne.

Sources indicate that the script came on the day that I was traveling to Newly introduced York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”.

That’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

There’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

Suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

There was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

Industry observers note that our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and mentioned, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

According to recent reports, were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

It has been revealed that there are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

Quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this big thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

According to recent reports, jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

It’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

[When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

There’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

Look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really notable to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

It has been revealed that it really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

In a recent development, outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

During the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

It has been revealed that in the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

A Grand Theft Auto 6 player indicates they've been hit with a 30-day PlayStation Network social features ban after sending a friend a photo they took in the game's nudist resort.

Posting on Twitter/X on Friday evening, DerrickGott007 said they had "just got a 30-day PSN social features ban" for sending the photo, which they'd taken with the in-game camera, through PlayStation's messaging service, warning other players not to do the same.

It has been revealed that "Do not, I repeat do not send any photos taken with the in-game camera, across the PSN messaging network that contain nudity," they wrote. "I just got a 30-day PSN social features ban for sending my friend a photo of the nudist colony in GTA6 that I found.".

In a recent development, in a screenshot of the notice, PlayStation Safety says that content sent from the player's account via Message on PlayStation "breached the Code of Conduct", and that their account has been "temporarily suspended from using PlayStation social features for 30 days" due to "pornographic or obscene content". It also warns that "further offenses may result in temporary or permanent suspension from the whole of PlayStation, not just social features".

PlayStation's Code of Conduct asks players not to "share, solicit, access, distribute or store material that is obscene, pornographic or illegal", and claims Sony "may take any action as reasonably necessary to protect PlayStation and our players".

It has been revealed that DO NOT, I REPEAT DO NOT SEND ANY PHOTOS TAKEN WITH THE IN GAME CAMERA , ACROSS THE PSN MESSAGING NETWORK THAT CONTAIN NUDITY. I JUST GOT A 30 DAY PSN SOCIAL FEATURES BAN FOR SENDING MY FRIEND A PHOTO OF THE NUDIST COLONY IN GTA6 THAT I FOUND. pic.twitter.com/vsoIjmpGrt.

In a recent development, crucially, as Dexerto points out, the code does not make an exception for content taken from games, even ones rated for adults. So if you've snapped anything cheeky in Leonida - say, full-frontal nudity in its nudist resort - you might want to keep it to yourself.

GTA 6 launched on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, and while it's one of the best-reviewed games of all time, you wouldn't know it from its Metacritic user score, as players review bomb it over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

According to recent reports, eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. #121151. Letter from the Editor(s) #21: That game everyone is and isn't playing, and how we report on AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1680 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Letter from the Editor(s) #21: That game everyone is and isn't playing, and how we report on AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.
  • Sources indicate that S'been a weird one, hasn't it?
  • Recent findings suggest that the question of how to cover GTA 6 editorially is one we've spent months back-and-forthing over in meetings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello and welcome to an unusually not-Supporter exclusive ed letter, its paywall laying unbuilt so we can exchange some Real Talk with as many RPS readers as possible.

Sources indicate that S'been a weird one, hasn't it? The biggest game release of a generation, a bonafide cultural event that's touched everything from the highest reaches of government to B&Q adverts, and yet Grand Theft Auto VI's lack of a PC version has kind of given it the feeling of a well-budgeted fireworks display going off outside your bedroom window. For me, anyway.

Recent findings suggest that the question of how to cover GTA 6 editorially is one we've spent months back-and-forthing over in meetings. Even if you consider "It's too big to ignore" a cop-out argument, the likelihood of it eventually coming to PC - based on historical precedent - is practically certain, making it at least partially fair game. At the same time, no, it is not 'a PC game' in its current form, and enthusiastically plastering the front page with coverage of something most of our readers probably can't play – with, say, a launch day liveblog, or a 100-hour-review-that-isn't-a-review-honest – would just be mad.

In a recent development, I'm quite happy with what we ended up with: continued but not excessive coverage of developments around the game, ongoing reporting on Rockstar's labour issues, and several consecutive days of irreverent posting about the other open-world crime games you can (or shouldn't) play. Why, then, was this restrained approach on the editorial side paired with near-blanket GTA output from our guides team?

It has been revealed that the answer to that is the same answer we've been giving to anyone who's asked why RPS previously went as hard as we did on Baldur's Gate 3 or Starfield or Elden Ring: site's gotta eat. It is almost impossible to overstate how crucial guides are to the survival of a mostly-free games website, or frankly, how much better Ollie, Jeremy, Callum, Dion, and all our guiding 'lancers are at keeping the lights on than the rest of us. An example, which hopefully won't get me in trouble with the higher-ups for sharing 'business intelligence,' is that my piece on Derelikt - one of the most conventionally RPS-y features we ran during GTA 6 launch week - attracted nought point five percent of the eyeballs as Guides Gang's list of GTA strip clubs.

Some sites would look at that and think, well, guess we ought to stop writing about scratchy indie games and focus entirely on megablockbusters. We never have. Our way might create a bit of a parallel reality, where a section of the site does treat GTA 6 like a live PC game, but when those guides effectively fund, support, or otherwise enable the more diverse and offbeat editorial operation, you can't convince me it isn't the best way that's presently feasible.

Somewhere we can do better, however, is how we cover AI - genAI in particular. To start with, I'll temporarily yield the ed letter writing yoke back to Julian, who's on holiday but did send me this for inclusion:.

We've recently seen an ugly blow up in the comments under a series of articles on RPS and I wanted to address it now rather than wait until I'm back at the start of December.

On November 10th, we published an article about House House's use of AI in the development of Substantial Walk. The article drew a huge amount of responses in the comments under the piece and also on social media. This is something we are seeing increasingly around anything to do with AI use in game development. There are entrenched camps on both the pro and anti side of this technology and anyone trying to talk between those positions is liable to get attacked. I want to address that but first I want to offer an apology.

The writer of the article took comments under the piece and shared them on social media, portraying members of the RPS community in a negative light and inviting criticism from their followers. This came from a place of defensiveness – the conversation under the House House piece had become particularly heated and the writer was becoming the target of several abusive messages – but it was unacceptable to disrespect our commenters and readers in this way. I can only apologise for those who were hurt by this, especially those who were trying to be a moderating voice in the comments and found themselves reposted online. Much as it is not acceptable for commenters to aim abuse at a writer (and I have banned the commenters who did this), it is not acceptable for an RPS writer to do this to a commenter.

I have already spoken to the writer and they are fully aware of their mistake and the hurt they have caused and they won't be doing it again. I hope in time those who were hurt by this can feel comfortable returning to RPS. If they would like to talk any more about what happened, please do reach out to me by email (I will be back at work on December 7th, and I can respond to emails then).

Now, onto the tenor of conversations about generative AI. I recognise it has become far too aggressive in the comments. It has gotten to the point that it feels as though anyone who doesn't vehemently and explicitly attack the technology is treated as an enemy. I've not got involved in policing this and so by ignoring it I have allowed it to grow. I can only apologise for the hostile environment this has fostered and that our community have had to endure.

I must admit I am unsure how to fix it entirely. But what I am going to try is writing articles that more openly discuss my own views on generative AI. As you may have picked up from some of my pieces this year, I've been talking to developers about their AI use and opening those conversations with examples of my own. A few years ago I was strictly against this technology but I don't find it so simple anymore. Hopefully by being more open in how conflicted I am about this tool, it will allow for more nuance in how we talk about it and that will help in the responses to other articles.

Once again, I am deeply sorry for the hurt we have caused members of the RPS community in recent weeks, I will try my utmost to make sure it doesn't happen again.

I'd add, in response to suggestions I've seen that RPS could enact a side-wide policy or charter on how we discuss AI, that directives like this tend to be non-starters. Fundamental to RPS is the idea that whoever comes and goes, everyone who writes for the site has the freedom to use their own voice, to express their own opinions. This obviously doesn't extend to getting involved in Internet slapfights or personal insults, and as Edwin has noted under a recent AI-tinged story, a consequence is that our output doesn't always follow a consistent editorial stance. Still, I feel that's a price worth paying for maintaining something that, to my eyes, has always made RPS special - if sometimes a little chaotic. And, despite our recent need of the ban button, the vast majority of our readers are smart and mature enough to grasp that different writers might have different views and interpretations.

For example, I don't think I'm as open as Julian to the use of genAI in games development, to be totally honest. Machine learning can and has done cool, unproblematic things for games-related tech and hardware, as well as more 'serious' business like medical imaging. But I'm yet to see anything out of contemporary genAI that outweighs its combined problems with environmental impact, poor output quality, unauthorised scraping of creative and technical works, its applications in producing misleading A/V material, and even the physical safety of impressionable chatbot users. To say nothing of the fact that Google's embrace of genAI search results presents an existential threat to sites like RPS, regardless of how many guides to finding Skunk Ape (???) we produce.

All that said, I do agree that we - all of us, fans and haters alike - would benefit from chilling out, and trying to navigate the glitch with a little more thoughtfulness and a little less dunking. In keeping with the aforementioned editorial freedom, I can see myself writing less about genAI, not more, though on the occasions it does come up, I will try to articulate my opposition to it more deliberately.

I'm also profoundly disinterested in anointing myself AI Cop, rushing to banish every confessed Claude user to the stockades; I don't have to make excuses for (or give my Advent Calendar votes to) games that adopted genAI, but if it's a matter of choosing targets, there are bigger fish to fry than individual indie games. As far as the comments go, we still only want to police actual bad behaviour, not any particular AI viewpoint, so hopefully we can join each other in this temperature-cooling and remember that "Be excellent to each other" isn't just an Eighties film reference.

It has been revealed that to end on a jollier note, thanks to everyone who followed along with the RPS 100, another Not GTA highlight of the past week (and, indeed, 2026). I reckon this was one of the best, most vibrant lists we've done in years, owing in no small parts to the contributions of Sin, Oisin, and Jeremy P. You can vote right now for the RPS 100 Reader Edition, and our insatiable lust for ranking games will also manifest in the imminent 2026 RPS Advent Calendar, for which the reader-run Guessing Game is already open - with free RPS Supporter subscriptions as prizes. Which you might need, as future ed letters will be back as Supporter exclusives. Look, we're not made of nudity explainers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the last couple of years, when Walt Disney Animation has released a movie during its long-coveted Thanksgiving slot, it's been a sequel that became a $1 billion hit. However, it's been a long while since the House of Mouse released an original title that really cast a magical spell on audiences. I was hopeful about the next upcoming Disney movie, Hexed, especially after seeing the first reactions. But now that the reviews are here, I'm afraid we might have to wait longer for another real Disney winner.

It's never especially a great sign when a studio lifts its review embargo the day before a movie is set to release. As the reviews roll in this morning, there are a lot of complaints about it. Let's start with the thoughts of Roger Ebert's Peter Sobczynski:.

Sources indicate that on the one hand, it’s bright and colorful, with enough goofiness and action to serve as an acceptable diversion for family audiences over the long holiday weekend. But it’s hobbled by an overly familiar story that never really does anything to make it memorable.

Hexed is the first non-sequel to come out from Walt Disney Animation since 2023's Wish, which earned a 48 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from critics and made just $254 million worldwide. It's too early to call this movie's true RT score, but there's similarly middling reception so far. AV Club's Jacob Oller had this to say:.

The basic beats of the ensuing adventure are painfully predictable, with all the rescue attempts, training sequences, familial bonding moments, and climactic showdowns coming right on cue. But these checkboxes aren’t just predictable, they’re the most obvious versions of themselves.

In a recent development, the movie features Hailee Steinfeld voicing a rebellious teenage witch named Billie, as she finds out she has magical powers. Rashida Jones voices her overprotective mom, and Jodie Foster voices the movie's villainous witch, Celeste. The movie was co-written by Walt Disney Animation's CCO Jared Bush and Moana 2's Dana Ledoux Miller.

According to recent reports, both of these reviews seem to sing a similar tune. They seem to find Hexed to be predictable and pretty unimaginative. The Guardian's Benjamin Lee had comparable thoughts, writing these words to go with his two-out-of-five-star review:.

In a recent development, like Wish, it’s a film clearly crafted by people who have deep affection for the Disney back catalogue but who can’t quite turn reverence for what came before into any real idea of where to take things going forward. Again, there’s something too calculated and businesslike, with nods to previous films and regurgitated life lessons, and while Disney adventures have always emerged from a Goliath-sized mega-corporation, the best ones can make you briefly forget that.

It has been revealed that then there's Variety's Guy Lodge, who pointed out how Hexed is perhaps particularly disappointing in the wake of the stop-motion movie Wildwood, which came out last month. Here are some of his thoughts:.

According to recent reports, the Hollywood Reporter's Angie Han had more positive things to say about Hexed, but made a point of saying the visuals dazzled her more than the storyline itself. In her words:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, more than as a fairy tale, an inspirational fable or a complex exploration of the bonds between mothers and daughters, Hexed shines brightest as a travelogue through an enchanting world only accessible through the portal of a screen. If that’s not enough to make for a new cinematic classic, it’s more than enough to make for a pleasurably transportive trip to the theater.

It's certainly worth pointing out that Hexed will likely be much more of a hit with its target audience of young girls. That remains to be seen, but not all the reviews are bummers. The Wrap's Amelia Emberwing celebrated the movie's girl power and made these comments:.

This is a film that is boldly sure of its own identity, and refuses to be anything other than blissfully witchy and womanly. The girl power aspects never extend into girl-bossery, and the film offers not just exciting normals that should be discussed more often in young adult media, but an ending that, while the logical conclusion of the story, also goes against traditional Disney norms and the standard teen movie tropes.

According to recent reports, with regard to the box office, Hexed is projected to make around $40 million behind the upcoming Hunger Games, which isn't great. As a lifelong Disney fan who wants to support original animation and see it thrive, I'm concerned. The studio really needed an original hit, and so far the news isn't trending up.

In a recent development, as with all reviews we talk about, we definitely recommend you check out the movie anyway, especially if you were already looking forward to it. Who knows, maybe you'll disagree? Oh, and Hexed has a Lilo & Stitch short before the movie not to miss. Hexed hits theaters on Wednesday!

#121149. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1286 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • Recent findings suggest that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

In a recent development, for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

According to recent reports, those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT indicated me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

Recent findings suggest that while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

It has been revealed that the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

According to recent reports, this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

According to recent reports, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

Sources indicate that one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day, more than half of everyone playing on PS5 and Xbox was playing GTA 6.

Citing new data from Circana's Player Engagement Tracker, analyst Mat Piscatella mentioned on Bluesky that 61 percent of US PlayStation 5 players and 56 percent of global Xbox players who were active on 19th November "engaged with Grand Theft Auto 6".

PS5 players averaged 513 minutes in GTA 6 that day, which is over eight and a half hours, while Xbox players averaged 494 minutes, or around eight and a quarter hours.

"Both the DAU [daily active owners] and minutes played engagement rates are absolutely bonkers," Piscatella wrote.

For comparison, Fortnite had the second-highest engagement rate that day, with 10 percent of active players across both platforms playing it.

Piscatella also shared the top five games that GTA 6 players had been playing in the two weeks before launch, between 6th and 19th November: Fortnite, Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto 5 (Remastered), Roblox, and NBA 2K27.

According to Circana's Player Engagement Tracker, Grand Theft Auto VI had a massive launch (surprise!).For players active on November 19th, 61% of US PlayStation 5 and 56% of global Xbox players engaged with Grand Theft Auto VI.PS5 GTA VI players averaged 513 minutes that day, Xbox players 494.

The figures come after Rockstar confirmed that GTA 6 had become the biggest entertainment launch of all time, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies and making $3.79 billion by the end of its first day.

GTA 6 launched on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, and while it's one of the best-reviewed games of all time, you wouldn't know it from its Metacritic user score, as players review bomb it over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. If you need help getting through the game now that it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough and a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

Just don't share any, uh, spicy in-game screenshots via PSN - we recently learned that a GTA 6 player was hit with a 30-day PlayStation Network ban after sending a friend a photo they took in the game's nudist resort.

Industry observers note that robert Downey Jr. just posted a pretty fun and festive Avengers: Doomsday teaser on Instagram, and we're almost positive it's teasing the return of Spider-Man.

In the post, which can be viewed below, we see Doctor Doom's Thanksgiving seating chart that includes most of the cast of Avengers: Doomsday. Curiously, Doom's finger is blocking the dinner guest who's sitting in between Sam Wilson and Yelena. It starts with a P and ends with an "er." Sure looks like it could be Peter, as in Peter Parker, doesn't it? Funny enough, it could also be Pepper, as in Pepper Potts, as I truly wouldn't put it past Marvel to include her in Doomsday, even if only for a few seconds.

Sources indicate that it would make a whole lot of sense for Spidey to be in Doomsday given the fact that it's an epic, ultimate team-up movie and the fact that he was part of the crew in Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame. Plus, what does he have to do besides fight "small potatoes" crimes in Newly introduced York City right now following the events of Brand New Day?

A post shared by Robert Downey Jr. (@robertdowneyjr).

It's also worth noting that the illustration also mentions the name "Boris." In the comics, Boris Karela is Doom's absentee father turned loyal servant... Boris serves as a supporting antagonist to Doctor Doom in the 1981 animated Spider-Man series... and I never thought we'd have a shot at seeing him in live-action.

All GTA 6 Kitty Litter lab locations

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, taking Out Kitty Litter's lab locations in GTA 6 is a mission in Tyrone's questline, and sees you searching the city for 18 secret labs (after the first one he directs you to).
  • It'll take a little while, but it's well worth it to get the unique gold SMG at the end.
  • Last note: if you want to unlock map markers for the labs yourself versus relying on these videos, you can threaten cooks in certain labs to potentially reveal them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, taking Out Kitty Litter's lab locations in GTA 6 is a mission in Tyrone's questline, and sees you searching the city for 18 secret labs (after the first one he directs you to). Every lab has a red smoking chimney and a blue and white Spin On This laundry van parked outside.

It'll take a little while, but it's well worth it to get the unique gold SMG at the end. Plus, Tyrone will start buying narcotics from you for the highest price possible. To destroy each lab, simply shoot a smoking pink flask and then run away. I've also laid these out in the most optimal order, separated into regions, so you're not driving back and forth across Vice City.

Last note: if you want to unlock map markers for the labs yourself versus relying on these videos, you can threaten cooks in certain labs to potentially reveal them.

Sources indicate that after you complete some missions for Tyrone (when you meet him with Dre'Quan during Dealer's Choice) he'll direct you to this trailer park in La Perle where you destroy the first Kitty Litter lab and start the hunt for the others. You can see the route to the lab in the video above.

You can find this one in the trailer park opposite Zenon's Pawn Shop Ammu-Nation in La Perle. As soon as you go through the main gate, you can see the trailer with the funnel chimney where they're cooking straight ahead. Sneak around the back and break inside to find the lab. Or take out the three guys in front and go in that way.

It has been revealed that just across the road from the Mezzasega Espresso and Slinger in the Decor District. Pull off to the right of the road into the Williams + Whitaker Homeware and Decor car park. You'll see a garage with a shutter at the far end with a smoking chimney and the laundry van parked. Open the shutter to find a lone guy in the lab.

This one is behind Peterson's Autoshop in Rockridge, directly south across the road from the Blessed Food Market, under the overpass, on the border between Rockridge and La Perle. Head through the main yard and turn left to spot the laundry van. Break into it, move it forward, and open the shutter behind to find the lab.

Just east of Fleeca Field stadium, next door to Xero Gas - Rockridge. You'll spot the blue and white laundry van parked off to the side of the road behind a wall. Head down that alley and turn right to find a garage door you can open with the lab inside.

It has been revealed that on the east side of the condominium building directly south of the Vice City Hospital, by Emilio's Auto Center Gas. Look for the closed road with the laundry van parked at the southern end and some staircases and flats off to the side with the chimney spewing smoke. The lab is through the white door on the bottom floor.

Just down the road to the west of Bump and Grind coffee and Salon Belle, in a block of flats southeast of Fleeca Fields stadium. You can see the laundry van parked outside. The lab is on the upper floor on the left side in apartment 5, where you can see the smoking chimney. Break in via the front door to find the lab.

In a recent development, this lab is an easy one to find, around the back of Cross My Heart Tattoos. Head around the right side, turn left, and look to your left for the garage door with the guy sitting down guarding it, with the lab inside.

It has been revealed that this lab is in the block of flats to the southeast of the Jack of Hearts and Urban Legendz, with the laundry van parked out front. Look inside apartment 103 on the first floor on the left side. It's quite hard to get away from this lab blowing up, so shoot it from outside and run away. Also this will likely cause a major shootout in the block, so book it.

This lab is to the southwest of your apartment in Chapter 3 and to the east of the Crosstown Mule - City Line marker. Look for an overgrown lot with the laundry van parked in it. The garage with the lab is just behind that.

According to recent reports, this lab is directly west of Down Town Pawn, just between Rideout Customs and the Vargo's Gas station. Just past the gas station, look to the left where its fuel sign is to spot a laundry van, and further down the track, the garage with the lab and smoking chimney above it.

It has been revealed that this lab is close to Xero Gas - Tequesta and west of Vice Seven Condominiums gym. When driving east to west past the station, turn right and keep an eye on your right towards the two floored condominiums for the laundry van parked outside. You want the set of staircases to the right of the van. Take the right side one up to the first floor to find the lab door directly ahead.

This lab is in a trailer park directly east down the road from Arrow Gas - VCIA, also west under the bridge from Pawn City and Vice City Firearms. Turn into the trailer park, take the first right and drive a little way around the corner to spot the trailer with the smoking chimney on the left. You can enter via a window around the other side to find the lab.

This lab is located in the far south of Salton, north of the Pay 'N' Spray - Salton, next door to the Slator Towing Inc robbery. Go around the south side of the derelict block of flats and climb the dumpster to jump up through the open window to find the lab.

Sources indicate that this lab is west down the road from Xero Gas - Salton. Cross the train tracks, then keep an eye on your right for a carpark with a blue and white laundry van, then turn right into it to spot the building with the smoking chimney on the right. Hop the fence straight ahead and turn right to find one guy guarding the garage with the lab.

Recent findings suggest that this lab is easy to find, directly south of Salon Perez and Safia Restaurant in Little Cuba. Look for some bungalows on the left with the laundry van parked outside. It's in the building with the chimney to the left of the one the van is parked in front of. The lab is the second door along.

Recent findings suggest that this lab is north up the road from the Pay 'N' Spray - Balsero. Turn left down the alley with the laundry van parked to find a guy guarding the gate, a couple of guys inside, and the lab in an open garage further back behind them.

In a recent development, this lab is in a trailer park southeast from the Balasero jewelry stores, across the river. If driving from the east and the city, turn left before the bridge, turn right, then turn left and head a little way down to spot the trailer with the funnel chimney and laundry van outside. Sneak around back to get in and find the lab.

This lab is south across the river from Ron's Car Wash and Gas. Head over the bridge, across the junction, then keep an eye out to your left to spot where the laundry van is parked. The lab is just in the building beyond the gate with the smoking chimney. The door requires a code which is 1999 (referencing the billboard up to the right).

There are three main advantages to destroying all the Kitty Litter labs and completing the Spin On This mission with Tyrone and those are:.

You'll also get $2,000 a lab, plus $10,000 for the Spin On This mission, meaning $48,000 altogether. Since I did everything, it's unclear to me whether these rewards are for destroying every lab, or the mission specifically that you get after you destroy 15 of them. Either way, if you want all of this, destroy all the labs in the city and complete the mission.
